title: Law & Order
subtitle: The justice system, courts, police, legal aid and the principles behind Canadian law

questions.question: What is the presumption of innocence?
options: Everyone is guilty until proven innocent
Everyone is innocent until proven guilty
Judges decide guilt before a trial
questions.explanation: Our judicial system is founded on the presumption of innocence in criminal matters, meaning everyone is innocent until proven guilty.

questions.question: What is "due process"?
options: The process for applying for citizenship
The principle that the government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to under the law
questions.explanation: Due process is the principle that the government must respect all the legal rights a person is entitled to under the law. The Canadian justice system guarantees everyone due process.

questions.question: Canada's legal system is based on a heritage that includes which of the following?
options: The rule of law, freedom under the law, democratic principles and due process
questions.explanation: Canada's legal system is based on a heritage that includes the rule of law, freedom under the law, democratic principles and due process.

questions.question: What is the role of the courts in Canada?
questions.explanation: Laws are made by elected representatives. The courts settle disputes and the police enforce the laws. The law applies to everyone, including judges, politicians and the police.

questions.question: What is Canada's highest court?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of Canada is our country's highest court. The Federal Court of Canada deals with matters concerning the federal government.

questions.question: Which court deals with matters concerning the federal government?
questions.explanation: The Federal Court of Canada deals with matters concerning the federal government.

questions.question: What are small claims courts for?
options: Civil cases involving small sums of money
questions.explanation: There are provincial courts for lesser offences, family courts, traffic courts and small claims courts for civil cases involving small sums of money.

questions.question: Which two provinces have their own provincial police forces?
questions.explanation: There are provincial police forces in Ontario and Quebec. The RCMP serves as the provincial police in all other provinces and territories, as well as in some municipalities.

questions.question: What is the role of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP)?
options: To enforce federal laws throughout Canada and serve as provincial police everywhere except Ontario and Quebec
questions.explanation: The RCMP enforce federal laws throughout Canada, and serve as the provincial police in all provinces and territories except Ontario and Quebec, as well as in some municipalities.

questions.question: In Canada, are you allowed to question the police about their service or conduct?
options: Yes. Almost all police forces have a process for bringing your concerns to them and seeking action
Only if you are a citizen
questions.explanation: You can question the police about their service or conduct if you feel you need to. Almost all police forces in Canada have a process by which you can bring your concerns and seek action.

questions.question: If you cannot afford a lawyer, what help is available?
options: Legal aid services, available free of charge or at low cost in most communities
The police will act as your lawyer
The judge pays for your lawyer
questions.explanation: Lawyers can help with legal problems and act for you in court. If you cannot pay, in most communities there are legal aid services available free of charge or at a low cost.

questions.question: What does the blindfolded Lady Justice symbolize?
options: The impartial manner in which laws are administered: blind to all considerations but the facts
That judges do not see the accused
questions.explanation: The blindfolded Lady Justice symbolizes the impartial manner in which our laws are administered: blind to all considerations but the facts.

questions.question: Who makes the laws in Canada?
questions.explanation: Laws are the written rules intended to guide people in our society. They are made by elected representatives.

questions.question: In most provinces, what is the trial court sometimes called?
options: The Court of Queen's (King's) Bench or the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: In most provinces there is an appeal court and a trial court, sometimes called the Court of Queen's Bench (now King's Bench) or the Supreme Court.

questions.question: What are Canada's laws intended to do?
options: Provide order in society, a peaceful way to settle disputes, and express the values and beliefs of Canadians
questions.explanation: Our laws are intended to provide order in society and a peaceful way to settle disputes, and to express the values and beliefs of Canadians.

questions.question: True or false: The law in Canada applies to everyone, including judges, politicians and the police.
questions.explanation: True. The law in Canada applies to everyone, including judges, politicians and the police. No one is above the law.

questions.question: True or false: Prisons have an essential role in punishing criminals and deterring crime.
questions.explanation: True. The guide states that prisons have an essential role in punishing criminals and deterring crime.

questions.question: True or false: You should only contact the police if you have committed a crime yourself.
questions.explanation: False. The police are there to keep people safe. You can ask for help after an accident, a theft, an assault, if you see a crime taking place, or if someone you know has gone missing.

questions.question: True or false: Municipal police departments exist in all provinces.
questions.explanation: True. There are municipal police departments in all provinces, and most major urban centres have municipal police forces.

questions.question: Why is serving on a jury described as a privilege?
options: Because jurors are paid very well
Because the justice system depends on impartial juries made up of citizens
Because it exempts you from voting
questions.explanation: Serving on a jury is a privilege that makes the justice system work, as it depends on impartial juries made up of citizens. When called, you are legally required to serve.
